questions.q: A person lifts a box, then carries it horizontally across the room while still applying an upwards force to hold it up. Why is no work done on the box while it is being carried across the floor?
options: The force on the box has dropped to zero once it is held up
The displacement of the box is at right angles to the upwards force, so the force does no work
The box is moving at constant speed, and constant speed always means zero work
Carrying the box does negative work that exactly cancels the lifting work
questions.explanation: Work is done only when a force gives a displacement in the direction of the force. While the box is carried across the floor the upwards force is at right angles to the horizontal displacement, so no work is done on it — just as pushing against a wall that does not move does zero work.

questions.q: A sled is dragged 100 m across ice by a tow rope that makes an angle of 30° to the horizontal. If a force of 70 N is applied to pull the sled, how much work is done?
working: Only the component of force in the direction of the displacement does work: \(F_{//} = F\cos\theta\)
questions.explanation: When the force is applied at an angle to the displacement, only the component \(F\cos\theta\) acting in the direction of motion contributes to the work. Here \(70\cos 30^\circ = 60.6\,\mathrm{N}\), and over 100 m that does 6060 J of work.

questions.q: Kinetic energy is the energy associated with the movement of an object. According to the work-energy relationship, the change in kinetic energy of an object is equal to which quantity?
options: The gravitational potential energy it has lost
The work done on it by the net force acting on it
Its mass multiplied by its acceleration
The total energy stored in the object at rest
questions.explanation: The change in kinetic energy equals the work done by the net force: \(\Delta E_k = F_{net}\,s\). Combining this with \(F_{net}=ma\) and the equations of motion gives the kinetic energy of a moving object as \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\).

questions.q: A 30 kg child sits at the top of a smooth slide whose vertical distance is 3 metres. Taking g as 9.8 m s⁻², calculate the child's gravitational potential energy at the top of the slide relative to the ground.
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential energy relative to the reference height is \(U_g = mgh\). For the 30 kg child 3 m above the ground that is \(30 \times 9.8 \times 3 = 882\,\mathrm{J}\), which is then available to transform into kinetic energy as the child slides down.

questions.q: The increase in gravitational potential energy of an object of mass m lifted through a height Δh is ΔUg = mgΔh. Why does this formula use the change in height Δh rather than an absolute height?
options: Because g changes so rapidly with height that absolute heights are meaningless
Because the formula only provides a way of calculating changes in gravitational potential energy, measured from whatever reference height is chosen
Because gravitational potential energy is always zero at the Earth's surface
Because mass decreases as the object is lifted
questions.explanation: The expression \(\Delta U_g = mg\Delta h\) comes from the work done against gravity, \(W = Fs = mg\Delta h\). It calculates a change relative to a chosen reference height (usually ground or floor level), so it is the change in height that matters, not an absolute position.

questions.q: When a tennis ball bounces on a hard surface it does not rebound to its original height, so mechanical energy is not conserved. Where has the missing mechanical energy gone?
options: It has been destroyed, violating conservation of energy in collisions
It is transformed to thermal energy of the air, ground and ball, with some lost as sound and permanent deformation
It is stored permanently as gravitational potential energy in the ground
It is converted entirely back into strain potential energy of the ball
questions.explanation: During each transformation in the bounce some mechanical energy becomes thermal energy (a small temperature rise), sound, or permanent deformation through breaking bonds. The energy is not destroyed — it is transformed into forms that are difficult to recover, which is why the efficiency \(\eta = \tfrac{\text{useful energy out}}{\text{total energy in}}\) is less than 100%.

questions.q: From memory, state the key summary points linking work, kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and power for this topic.
keyPoints: Work is done when energy is transferred by a force; it is the product of the force and the displacement in the direction of the force.
The work done by the net force equals the object's change in kinetic energy, where \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\).

The change in gravitational potential energy is \(\Delta U_g = mg\Delta h\); kinetic and gravitational potential energy are forms of mechanical energy, usually taken as conserved in a mechanical interaction.
Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or work is done, and the power delivered by a force equals the force times the velocity (P = Fv).
questions.explanation: These are the chapter summary statements. If you recalled work as force times displacement, the work-energy link to \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), \(\Delta U_g = mg\Delta h\), conservation of mechanical energy, and power as both rate of work and Fv, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or transformed. The power delivered when a force F is applied to an object moving at velocity v can be expressed as which of the following?
options: \(P = Fv\), derived from \(P = \tfrac{W}{\Delta t} = \tfrac{Fs}{\Delta t}\) with \(v = \tfrac{s}{\Delta t}\)
\(P = \tfrac{F}{v}\), measured in joules
\(P = F\Delta t\), measured in watts
questions.explanation: Starting from \(P = \tfrac{W}{\Delta t} = \tfrac{Fs}{\Delta t}\) and recognising that speed \(v = \tfrac{s}{\Delta t}\) gives \(P = Fv\). The SI unit of power is the watt, defined as 1 J s⁻¹.

questions.q: A student says 'the car's kinetic energy is lost when it brakes to a stop.' From memory, explain what is wrong with this statement and how it should be phrased.
keyPoints: The kinetic energy is not lost or used up — it is transformed.
Friction in the brakes converts the car's kinetic energy into thermal energy (heating the pads and discs), with a little into sound.
By the law of conservation of energy, energy cannot be destroyed, only transformed, so the total energy is conserved.
Markers penalise 'lost' or 'used up' — say 'transformed into heat by friction in the brakes'.
questions.explanation: This is the single most important piece of energy language in the course: energy is transformed, not destroyed. If you caught the 'transformed not lost' point and named friction to heat, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of energy transformations, what happens to the kinetic energy of a car as it brakes to a stop, and why it is incorrect to say the energy is destroyed. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: As the car brakes, friction between the brake pads and discs transforms the car's kinetic energy into thermal energy, heating the brakes, with a small amount becoming sound. The kinetic energy is therefore transformed into other forms, not destroyed. It is incorrect to say the energy is destroyed because the law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another; the total energy is conserved throughout.

criteria.descriptor: States the kinetic energy is transformed to heat (thermal energy) by friction in the brakes.
Refers to the law of conservation of energy — energy cannot be created or destroyed.
Concludes the energy is transformed, not destroyed, and the total energy is conserved.

questions.explanation: The marks reward the 'transformed, not destroyed' distinction and explicit naming of the conservation of energy principle. Avoid the words 'lost' or 'used up', which markers penalise.
